nameStory: The name 'groundsel tree' comes from an old English word meaning 'ground swallower,' referring to how this shrub can quickly colonize disturbed soil. Despite being called a 'tree,' it's actually a shrub that rarely grows taller than 12 feet, showing how common names can sometimes be misleading!
description: Groundsel tree is a hardy native shrub that thrives in salty, coastal conditions where many other plants struggle. It grows 6-12 feet tall with a somewhat scraggly, irregular shape and thick, leathery leaves that feel waxy to the touch. In fall, female plants become absolutely spectacular when covered in fluffy white seed heads that look like cotton balls scattered across the branches. This tough shrub is a member of the sunflower family, though its small flowers look nothing like the classic daisy shape most people expect.

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: In fall, female plants explode with masses of bright white, fluffy seed heads that feel cottony and catch the light beautifully - this is the most eye-catching feature

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, leathery leaves that feel waxy and slightly sticky, with coarse teeth along the edges - they're alternate and wedge-shaped, widest toward the tip

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Scraggly, multi-stemmed shrub 6-12 feet tall with irregular branching - often looks somewhat unkempt compared to cultivated shrubs

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, inconspicuous whitish flowers in clusters that lack petals - male and female flowers are on separate plants, blooming in late summer

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Grayish-brown bark that's fairly smooth on younger stems, becoming slightly furrowed with age - stems feel sturdy and woody

habitat: Groundsel tree loves salty, disturbed soils near the coast - you'll find it thriving in salt marshes, beach edges, roadside ditches, and abandoned lots within a few miles of the ocean. It's particularly common along the Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut coasts, where it can handle salt spray and sandy soils that challenge most other shrubs. Look for it in sunny, open areas rather than shaded forests.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as thick, waxy wedges - this is when the plant looks its neatest before summer growth makes it scraggly.
seasonality.summer: Small, unremarkable flowers bloom in clusters in late summer, with male and female flowers on separate plants looking quite different.
seasonality.fall: This is showtime! Female plants become covered in spectacular white, cottony seed heads that persist for weeks and are visible from far away.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the irregular growth pattern, though some seed heads may persist into early winter if not blown away.

funFact: Groundsel tree is one of the few shrubs that can actually improve soil quality in salt marshes by filtering excess salt from its leaves - the plant literally sweats salt crystals that you can sometimes see sparkling on the leaf surfaces on sunny days!
confusionNotes: The cottony fall seed heads might be confused with clematis seed heads, but clematis is a vine, not a shrub. The thick, waxy leaves are quite different from most other coastal shrubs - if it feels like you could write your name in the waxy coating, you've probably found groundsel tree.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'groundsel tree,' this plant is unrelated to the true groundsels (Senecio species) and isn't actually a tree. Many of its other common names like 'sea myrtle' and 'saltbush' better reflect its coastal habitat, though it's also not related to true myrtles or saltbushes - common names can be wonderfully confusing!
compareHints: Groundsel tree is the only Baccharis species naturally occurring in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Within the sunflower family, it's unusual for being a woody shrub rather than an herbaceous plant, and for having such inconspicuous flowers followed by such showy seed heads. Unlike most Asteraceae family members, you'd never mistake its flowers for typical daisies or sunflowers.
